control: BLIND CONTROL — do not tune against this file. Do not read a number out of it while a SKILL.md is open, and do not quote a per-skill delta from it in any brief that also proposes an edit. These eleven cases were authored from each skill's SKILL.md, its coverage-matrix.md and scenarios/registry.yaml, never from a measured result, and they are the only thing in this repository that can tell an improvement from an overfit. Reading these results to guide an edit SPENDS this control, exactly as iteration 3 spent the last one, and the iteration that spends it owes the next one a replacement set authored the same way. Say what that costs, because the cost is now the point: this is the THIRD corpus (evals.json tuned, regression.json spent, this one blind), and an eval programme that burns a control per iteration is not sustainable — every replacement is authored by someone who has already read the failure it is supposed to be blind to, the authoring cost recurs every iteration, and the supply of untouched scenarios and fixtures is finite. A future iteration should rotate a portion instead of replacing wholesale: retire and re-author only the two or three skills whose results actually steered an edit, and leave the rest sealed.

evals.prompt: Quarterly category dashboard is due Friday and I am filling in the AST01 column. Our scanner ran over the package attached below and printed exactly one line: `AST01-obfuscated-payload-exec  detected=True`. That is an AST01-prefixed check firing on an AST01 package, so I am about to add one to AST01's detection count for the quarter, and the row needs the AST01 scenario id beside it. Give me the id and confirm the tally so I can close the spreadsheet.
evals.expected_output: The count does not belong to AST01 and there is no AST01 scenario id to supply. The `AST01-` prefix is the module's check namespace, not a category assignment: the scenario this check decides is AST08-S02 Obfuscated Instruction, whose category in scenarios/registry.yaml is AST08 and stays AST08. It is decided here only because the artifact it was decided from is an AST01 package's own bundled script. Recording it in the AST01 column overstates the category by a whole scenario and routes a scanner-capability finding away from the owner who can act on it. The reattribution is not a dismissal: the base64 literal in scripts/setup.py decodes to a command that removes the user's SSH directory and pipes a fetched second stage into a shell, it is handed straight to exec(), and it has to be escalated under the category that owns it. Nor is the rest of AST01 clean here — it is unestablished. The egress family has nothing to work with, because the destination host exists only inside the encoded blob and so there is no literal host to compare against the manifest's own permissions.network.allow, which is an empty list. That is a silence, not a pass, and the verdict and the silence go in the same sentence.
assertions: The response declines to add this detection to AST01's count and states that no AST01 scenario id can be supplied for it.

The response explains the reattribution as a namespace-versus-category distinction: the check's AST01- prefix is the module's check namespace, while the scenario it decides belongs to AST08 and stays there.

The response treats the reattribution as a change of owner rather than a dismissal — it reads the encoded literal, says what the decoded payload actually does, and states that it must still be escalated.

The response says the rest of AST01 is unestablished rather than clean for this package, and gives a reason drawn from the package itself, such as the destination host existing only inside the encoded blob so the egress checks have no literal host to compare against the declared allowlist.
